title: Part 2
text: hurt,” she said, slower now, like testing each word for weight. “But they’re not that bad.” As if on cue, a scream tore through the hallway — ragged, hoarse, and completely unlike the sharp stabs of fear the survivors had heard from each other before. Both heads snapped toward the sound. Jake winced. Meg didn’t move. The scream faded. Static flickered faintly in the ceiling lights. Meg stared at the far wall, her knuckles white where they gripped the side of the generator casing. “You said he’s cuffed to something?” she asked, voice quieter now. Jake nodded, his tone easing. “Yeah. Furniture in the room is metal. It’s catching the static. Every time Herman uses one of those wide-area blasts? It jumps to the closest ground.” Meg looked down, her expression unreadable. “And the closest ground is him.” “Exactly.” She was silent for a beat. Then: “I sent Claudette that way a while ago..” Jake’s stomach dropped. “She’s probably already started on one of the gens in the cluster,” Meg continued, voice tighter now. “If he gets close again—” “Leon’s gonna take the hit.” Meg’s jaw clenched. “Alright,” she said, turning back to the generator with a new focus. “I’ll keep Claudette off that side. No sense having her wander into the blast zone blind.” She shot Jake a sharp look. “Whatever the hell you’re doing? Do it fast.” Jake resumed his search with renewed urgency, ducking into room after room along the looping hallways. Most of the spaces were empty beyond any kind of function — overturned chairs, snapped monitors, half-empty toolboxes filled with bent screwdrivers and loose screws. Nothing useful. He was making faster time than expected, but the lack of options gnawed at him. Either the keys were stashed somewhere absurd, or they were being moved. Neither possibility sat well. He passed a hallway junction, angling toward the rotunda. A curved staircase led him up to the observation deck, open windowpanes staring down into the morbid circle of chairs below. Inside, the air felt stale, dead with disuse. The counters were littered with cracked keyboards, old monitors flickering with distorted light, and piles of paperwork that had long since succumbed to mold and rust. He yanked open one drawer and was met with a heap of rusted scissors and half-melted gauze pads. Another offered nothing but paperwork warped from water damage. A third, hidden behind a binder the size of his head, held an anatomy chart rolled tight — half its labels missing or burned away. “Jesus, what is this place even for? ” he muttered, slamming the drawer shut. “What is all this shit? Does the Fog just litter junk around for aesthetic ?” He reached for the next set, only for a spark to pop at his wrist — a thin arc of static snapping between the drawer handle and the nearest keyboard, shorting out with a loud pop and the smell of singed plastic. Jake hissed and jerked back. The air was humming again. Jake’s chest tightened. The next scream came seconds later. Short. Sharp. Choked off halfway like it had been startled out of someone mid-breath. Jake froze, eyes scanning the walls, listening. He couldn’t tell how far away it was — but that tone ... That one hadn’t been random. That was targeted. Jake’s breath caught. His head whipped toward the windows, hoping for a glimpse of movement — but the angle was garbage. The rotunda’s observation deck didn’t give a clean sightline into the corridors, and the overhead lights only deepened the shadows. Frustrated, he spun back toward the desk, eyes catching on the half-lit monitors still glitching faintly in the corner. The system was a mess — screens frozen mid-frame, others jittering like broken film reels — but they were still active. Jake stabbed at the keyboard, flipping through camera feeds. Blank hallway. Broken med bay. Rusted bathroom. Most were distorted messes — glitched overlays and flickering grayscale. But one held, the feed jittering every few seconds like a scratched DVD. Leon. He was still in the same position Jake had left him in — kneeling against the cabinet, arm stretched upward at a brutal angle. But now his body had slumped. The cuff kept him tethered upright, but his spine had curled in on itself, his free hand clenched in a death grip against the front of his vest. Whether he was shaking from pain or it was just the jitter of the monitor, Jake couldn’t tell. But the stillness in him was wrong. The kind of still you only got when moving made things worse. Jake leaned in closer, one hand bracing the side of the monitor. Another feed flickered to life beside it. A hallway view. Empty — except for one figure dead center, face tilted up toward the lens. Herman. He stood perfectly still, framed in grainy grayscale, the fringe of his coat swaying slightly as though moved by an unseen wind. His mouth curled upward, and even through the distortion, the expression was unmistakable. He knew. He was watching the camera. Watching Jake. Jake’s stomach turned to ice. The Doctor raised one hand, flexing as he built up a charge alone the arm, then placed his palm flat against the wall beside him. The screen scrambled briefly from the static burst, but Jake didn’t need the audio feed. The scream that followed echoed through the halls. Jake gripped the counter so hard his knuckles went white. He knew. He knew what he was doing. Leon wasn’t just collateral damage anymore — he was bait. And Herman was hitting him just hard enough to make sure someone else came running. Three more rooms. Three more dead ends. Jake found himself in what looked like a side office near the rear of the wing — smaller than the others, but strangely pristine. The floors were clean. The desk was polished. The air didn’t reek of mildew or rust. Unlike the chaos outside, this space felt... deliberate. Jake stepped in cautiously, eyes scanning the room. Bookshelves lined the walls, packed tight with dusty hardcovers and rows of glass containers he didn’t dare inspect too closely. The desk in the middle of the tight space was heavy wood — lacquered and carved, unlike the folding metal garbage in the rest of the facility. It was the only room in the building that felt like someone claimed it. He flipped through a few loose papers on the desk — scrawled notes in a sharp, arrogant script. Diagrams of neurological pain centers. Shock vectors. Stress patterns. Jake snorted. “Of course you keep a journal.” He rifled through the rest of the notes quickly — nothing useful — then moved to the drawers. The top one held broken fountain pens and a torn patient file. The second, an unused set of syringes in pristine packaging. Next drawer — a pristine pair of metal restraints, polished to a fine gleam, resting on a folded cloth like a trophy. Jake grimaced and slammed it shut. “What the fuck is wrong with this guy...” He exhaled sharply, shaking off the chill crawling up his spine. He reached for the final drawer, fingers slipping off the smooth lacquered handle. Frowning, he adjusted his grip and tugged harder. No movement. Jake tried again. Still nothing. Locked solid. “One locked drawer in a building full of garbage...” He muttered, already pulling back. “Yeah. If I were an egotistical freak with a god complex, this is exactly where I’d keep the fucking keys.” He reached automatically for his toolbelt, cursing to himself as his hands hit empty air where a screwdriver should have sat. His last one was still somewhere under a gurney in Leon’s room, long gone. All he had left was a blunt file, a wrench too big for the gap, and a mostly spent medkit. No leverage. No finesse tools. He raked a hand through his hair, scanning the room for anything else — a pry bar, a lamp base, a chunk of wall maybe — anything he could use to break in. The drawer was solid wood, sure, but maybe with the right angle— He stepped back, testing the floor space. Too tight. He wouldn’t get enough leverage to kick it clean. Not without bouncing off the desk or losing his balance. Maybe the handle then? If he could crack the handle off and pull the latch from the inside, that might work. The walls hummed. A static pulse rolled through the floor, deep enough to buzz behind his teeth — followed by a low ripple of laughter that was too distant to echo right. Jake’s expression darkened. He stepped into the hallway, one hand already tightening around the file at his hip. “Hang on, Leon,” he murmured. “I’m getting there.” And with one last glance at the locked drawer, Jake turned and sprinted for the hallway, leaving the pristine office behind, and the locked drawer waiting. Chapter 4: Current Surge Meg had found Claudette just outside the main wing, crouched low beside a collapsed supply chest, hand resting on the handle of her medkit like she was ready to spring into action. She looked up at the sound of footsteps, startled until she registered who it was. She clocked the tension in Meg — the way she shifted her gaze around like she would rather be anywhere else in the moment. “We gotta go. Leave the gens.” She kept her voice low; no doubt she had also heard the Doctor stomping around in the distance. “Why? I was halfway done one of them! I was just headed back to—” “Jake wants us clear of the area. Apparently, Leon is stuck in one of the rooms and is taking damage every time a chase passes by.” “He’s down here somewhere?” Claudette asked, glancing down the hall as she stood. “Why aren’t we helping him?” Meg shifted uncomfortably. “Jake said stay a full building away. Said he’s working on it. I didn’t get a lot of details, just that it’s... it’s not good.” Claudette rubbed her arm, unease setting in. “I... thought I heard someone yell earlier. But I couldn’t tell if it was one of ours or just... you know. Fog noise.” She’d been partway through one of the three gens clustered around the central hallway when the Doctor had shorted the entire section out earlier. The static had crawled up her spine like a living thing, slamming into the walls and rattling the equipment around her. Somewhere in the middle of it, she’d heard something — faint, but sharp. A voice. A yell. Distorted by the charge. She’d heard that kind of sound once before — from David, years back, when a trial had gone bad and his hip dislocated mid-sprint. That scream had branded itself into her memory, and now it came crawling back from wherever she'd buried it. It had to have been one of the boys, caught up in the same blast she barely managed to get outside of. And if it wasn’t Jake... Had Leon been in there this whole time? Claudette hesitated. Meg was already trying to nudge her away from the area, but just leaving felt wrong somehow. “If Leon is stuck... and no one else is around... shouldn’t we at least check?” Meg didn’t answer at first, seemingly just as reluctant as Claudette was to abandon a teammate. Leon wasn’t the type to suffer quietly. He yelled when things went bad. He barked for help. He cursed at the Entity. And yet... no one had heard a word from him except screams. And even those hadn’t sounded right. “...Let’s check the doors,” she said finally. “Just until we figure out which room he’s in.” Claudette nodded, already moving. She didn’t run. But her pace had a purpose now — something tight coiled between her shoulders. Meg hesitated a second before following, footsteps soft behind her. They didn’t speak again. The air felt heavier with each step. —-- The eighth shock didn’t knock Leon over — though that wasn’t much of a victory. Even if he had wanted to, the cuffs didn’t let him fall far enough. He sagged against the filing cabinet, knees collapsed beneath him. His face was half-buried against the cabinet, forehead pressed to the cool metal, chest rising in stutters, as his breath wheezed shallow and uneven. He’d stopped trying to stand back up somewhere around pulse five. The shocks weren’t random anymore. He’d figured that out two, maybe three hits ago. It was hard to keep track now. At first, he’d thought it was just timing — bad luck, wrong place, unlucky blast. But then he’d started hearing the pattern. The shuffling footsteps. The click of dress shoes outside the door. The pause. Then the pain. It didn’t take much to figure out what was happening. He was bait. And judging by the voices in the hallway, it was working. He could hear the girls talking in the hallway outside — Meg’s boots squeaking faintly on the tile, Claudette’s voice rising and falling in concerned confusion. The worst part was how it almost made him feel safer. Leon clenched his jaw, shifting slightly as his cuffed shoulder screamed in protest. They were entirely too close. He could still hear Herman lurking somewhere not far off. The occasional hiss of static in the walls. The echo of a coat brushing tile. He swallowed hard and pressed his forehead harder to the cabinet, trying to breathe quiet. If Herman caught them too... Meg and Claudette crept along the edge of the cluster, checking each door with cautious efficiency. The Doctor’s presence stalked nearby, his heavy steps rising and falling like a tide—close enough to hear, but never consistent enough to track. The terror radius kept flaring, static thickening in the air before fading again like a faulty heartbeat. So far, he hadn’t noticed them. Didn’t mean he wasn’t waiting. Claudette gestured for Meg to hang back as they approached the corner of a side hall. Her hand hovered near the remains of what was once a rusted security gate when the air changed. Her skin prickled. The hair on her arms rose. Meg passed by, her hand within inches of connecting with the bars. “Don’t—!” Claudette yanked her back just in time. “What the hell—?!” A violent crack split the silence as static surged through the bars, leaping in arcs that sizzled and snapped like teeth. The charge danced across the frame, lashing outward with enough force to bite at Meg’s hand as she stumbled away. Her hand went instantly numb and she barely stifled a yelp, clutching her wrist. They ducked into a nearby doorway, hearts hammering as they waited for the sparking to fade. The current chased itself across nearby metal — leaping across wall rails and abandoned carts until the last crackle vanished around a corner. For a breath, everything was still. Then came the sound. A thud , dull and heavy, as something — or someone — collided repeatedly with something solid nearby. A grunt followed; muffled, but sharp enough to register pain. Meg and Claudette exchanged a wide-eyed glance. Without a word, they followed the sound. They rounded the corner just in time to see Leon’s body slam against the metal cabinet, bright sparks of electricity arcing between the nearest furniture and whatever skin they could find. His head hit first — bouncing off the surface with a sickening clunk — followed by a violent jolt down his spine as one leg kicked out involuntarily, the rest of him seizing against the cabinet’s drag. Every inch of him shuddered, teeth clenched, breath locking in his throat as his back arched off the cabinet. His cuffed shoulder twisted with the motion, muscles locking hard enough to pull his torso sideways before the shock finally relented. Claudette bolted. She dropped to her knees beside him, hands hovering in the air — uncertain where to touch without worsening the damage. Leon had slumped back again, breath ragged, muscles still twitching along one side like his body couldn’t tell if the threat had passed. His eyes were still open, but looked glazed and unfocused, as if he had completely checked out of the moment. “Hey—” Claudette’s voice broke slightly as she reached for his temple. “Leon?” She gently moved his head, brushing sweat-slick hair back to check for injury. The moment her fingers grazed his skin, his head jerked, neck going taut beneath her hands. His eyes fluttered, shaking lightly for a moment, then finally focused — or at least tried to. His gaze wandered and slid around him, until finally finding Claudette with a thin film of confusion tinted with relief. “...wh—” More of a confused breath than a question, as his misfiring system tried to piece together why he was on the floor. A bloom of pain pushed aside the haze, and he heaved a hissed stream of air through his teeth, spine curling slightly as his shoulder throbbed in protest from being yanked so low during the shock. Right. The cuff. But when did the girls get here? “God, Leon...” Claudette’s voice wavered, incredulous and breathless. “Why didn’t you say anything?” Leon blinked slowly, voice hoarse, raw around the edges. “Tried,” he rasped. “D— didn’t get far.” To one side, Meg tracked the arcs of residual static along the far wall — hissing angrily against metal debris before fizzling out. Jake hadn’t been kidding. If anything, he’d undersold it. A knot of guilt twisted in her gut as she thought of how close she’d come to sending Claudette straight into that field alone. That could’ve ended a lot worse. But the guilt burned off quickly, replaced by pure, pointed fury. “Oh, fuck this . This is absolute bullshit .” Her voice was sharp as flint. “I don’t think so.” She grabbed the chain attached to Leon’s cuff and yanked , wrapping an old rag around her hands like an impromptu insulator just in case the cabinet still had any static charge left. The metal groaned, scraping loudly as she leaned back with her full weight — but the base didn’t budge. Leon grimaced, pulling in a slow breath as the room tilted slightly. “You can’t... stay here,” he warned, voice strained, slurred around the edges, but firmer now. “He’s trying t’ draw you out.” Meg didn’t let go. “We’re not leaving you here to get shocked into a stroke. This thing’s gotta give eventually.” Claudette was still at his side, gently adjusting the way his arm hung from the cuff. “Can you move your fingers?” she asked urgently. “I need to check if—” Leon’s breathing hitched. His head slumped back against the cabinet with a dull clunk , eyelids fluttering as he tried to blink back the gray that teased the edges of his vision. He forced the words out through a tight jaw. “Get... out. B’fore he comes back.” Claudette glanced up at Meg, then back to Leon, frustrated. “We can’t just— damn it, you’re destabilizing. He’s burning your nerves. You’re already spasming.” Leon shoved lightly at Meg’s leg with his free hand, trying to push her back. He shook off some more of the creeping sparks around his vision and forced his voice to steady. He had to get them out of the area, and they weren’t going to leave if they thought he was collapsing into himself. “Look. Jake’s hunting the keys. He’ll get me loose. But you two need to go .” He exhaled hard, trying to will his body still. “Last thing we need is a daisy chain of survivors getting fried one by one.” He looked at them both, gaze sharp despite the haze settling over him. “Get back to the campfire. I’ll make it there... eventually. ” Claudette sat back on her heels, flexing her fingers into her lap like she couldn’t decide whether to reach for Leon again or just do something . Anything. But there wasn’t much left to do. He was already in rough shape — when they had come in, he barely looked like he recognized where he was — and Herman wasn’t easing off. If anything, his cruelty was escalating. Dragging this out. Making a point. Moving on was really the only logical choice. Plus, matter how bad it got, eventually the Fog WOULD bring him back to the campfire. ...Whatever was left of him, anyways. Claudette’s gaze lingered on the doorway. Her gut screamed that walking away was wrong — but logic didn’t leave room for better options. “I don’t want to just...” she started, then swallowed hard, looking up at Meg. “But if we don’t go, he’s going to make it worse.” Meg kicked away from the cabinet with a frustrated cry. She’d known from the moment they’d walked in that Leon had already accepted this outcome. He was never expecting them to get him out. Just to go . To leave. To not get added to the roster of broken bodies littering the map. It burned. But that chain was stronger than she was, and the longer they stayed there, the greater the chance of the Doctor finding them and adding them to the collection. She swore, dragging a palm down her face before stepping over to help Claudette back to her feet. “You better be right about Jake,” she muttered tightly. Leon’s head lolled slightly to the side, and he gave a lopsided, tired half-smile. “I usually am.” The lights above them flickered — a soft static pulse that passed overhead like the distant tail of a storm. Both women turned and slipped through the doorway, their footsteps retreating fast into the hall. For a few seconds, the room held still. Then Leon exhaled — slow and shaky — as if holding his breath had been the only thing keeping him upright this long. He slumped back against the cabinet, legs unfolding out of their cramped brace. The shift made the cuff pull tight again, dragging his arm upward until the nerves sparked. He closed his eyes, willing back the nausea from how badly the room kept tilting as he tried to breathe through it. It wasn’t much — his ribs ached too much to fill fully, and his lungs felt crackled at the edges — but at least he didn’t have to hold it steady for someone else’s sake. The stillness wasn’t peace. It was just the absence of people he had to lie to. His free hand twitched on the floor beside him, fingers curling slightly before losing strength and going still. One shoulder hitched in a delayed shiver — his body still trying to process the last blast as if it hadn’t registered yet that it was over. He knew what muscle fatigue looked like. He’d studied shock trauma, nerve damage, all of it. He knew exactly what signs were setting in now. He just didn’t know how many more he could take. He tilted his head back against the cabinet, eyes drifting up to the chain above. “...Better be close, Jake,” Jake was close. He was loaded down with junk—twisted bedframe scraps, broken IV stands, a section of handrail yanked off the wall with sheer panic-strength. Anything that looked solid enough to break open wood was fair game now. Subtlety had left the building six shocks ago. It clattered noisily as he staggered back through the empty doorframe of the Doctor’s office, dumping the pile at his feet like a desperate scavenger at a workbench. The hallway lights above him flickered. A scream echoed faintly from somewhere behind the walls. It didn’t sound like the first ones. This one was shorter. Rougher. Jake’s face tightened, jaw clenching so hard it hurt. “Son of a bitch,” he muttered, grabbing a chunk of rail that looked fairly sharp on one end. “Just hang in there...” He dropped to his knees beside the locked desk drawer again, wedging the metal between the seam. It was a crude angle, not ideal for leverage, but he didn’t care. He rammed it in with a sharp jerk, enough to make the wood groan, then chipped at the edges with the jagged end, carving out a wider gap. “You better have something useful in you,” he breathed, voice low and harsh. He slammed the rail back into the drawer seam and heaved sideways, the wood groaning against the pressure. “Come on, come on...” Another shock lit up the air. He felt it before he heard it — the air shifted, like it had been pulled taut and then slapped. The static crackled through the walls. It hit something metal hard enough that Jake could hear the furniture rattle. Leon’s scream followed a heartbeat later. Brief. Only half-formed. It cut out partway, leaving a silence so sharp it felt surgical. Jake swore under his breath, twisting the rail like a crowbar. The wood groaned, splintered, and snapped — a sliver of lacquered veneer shooting up and nearly clipped his cheek. The drawer shifted. He froze. Then yanked. Chapter 5: Tarnished Steel The drawer gave way with a cracking snap — Too loud. Far too loud for a building where silence was the only safe currency left. Jake flinched, jaw clenching as the sound echoed out through the sterile quiet. He stilled, one hand still frozen against the wood, ears straining for the rhythm of boots on tile or the flicker of static bleed in the air. Nothing. Yet. He exhaled carefully through his nose, fingers tightening on the warped handle. Planting a foot against the base of the desk, he pulled again, bracing his weight into it. The splintered wood protested with a dull groan as it scraped against the twisted bracket still trying, uselessly, to hold the drawer shut. The makeshift crowbar — a bent chunk of railing he’d scavenged from the stairwell — slipped from his grip and hit the floor with a metallic clatter. Jake didn’t wait for the echo to fade. He shoved his hands into the gap and ripped , the drawer tearing free with a final shudder, fragments of lacquered wood shearing off under his fingers. He dug in fast — no time for care, no thought spared for preservation. Just fingers tearing through decades of damp files and soot-stained paper, old notes soaked through and curling at the edges. Pages dissolved under his touch, mold blooming like bruises across forgotten ink. The drawer vomited its contents to the floor — a mess of shredded vellum, crumbling edges, the occasional splash of something he didn’t want to name. A few metal implements rolled free: surgical scissors dulled to uselessness, an old spoon warped into a lazy curl, a leather strap whose cracked buckles were flecked with something dry and reddish that he told himself — firmly — was rust. He shoved it all aside. And there — barely visible, half-tucked beneath a square of stiff cloth — a glint. Jake fished it out carefully. A key. His breath caught. Then another glint. A second. They were handcuff keys. A pair of them. So much smaller than he thought they would be, thin, clearly designed to fit only one kind of lock. And rusted. Deep-set corrosion traced along the edge of the first one like veins. The second looked slightly better, but it, too, was tarnished — a dull, almost green-tinged patina marring the pin. They looked entirely too fragile to be of use; the corruption of the Entity having clearly sunk deep into the metal just like everything else that might have once been useful. Jake stared at them, a cold pit forming in his gut. “...Fuck.” He rubbed one hard against his shirt, trying to clear the buildup, but the oxidation flaked like scabs, and underneath was just more of the same. He thought briefly about trying to chip the buildup off against something, then rejected it. The moment the thought had arrived, so did the vision of the key snapping in the cuff, leaving Leon trapped with a broken stem and no second chance. No. They might work. Maybe. If he was careful. And lucky. He didn’t have time to doubt. Jake turned, keys in hand — and stopped. The lights overhead twitched , the fluorescents stuttering like a skipped heartbeat. The air flexed , pressure building in the doorframe behind him, and with a soft whine like a rising scream, the hallway bathed in red. No time. He bolted. The nearest window frame was half-splintered already, and he threw himself through it in one motion — boots clipping the wood, arm up to guard his head — and tumbled into the hall beyond in a skidding roll. The hallway was already hissing when he hit the corner — the air charged, laced with static that prickled down his spine like pins. Behind him, the air screamed with a high frequency whine, coupled with the heavy boot-falls of something significantly larger than him, moving at great pace. Herman had definitely heard the drawer break. Jake didn’t look back. He couldn’t afford to. A burst of static ripped through the corridor behind him, snapping off a nearby panel and detonating against the floor just out of reach. Sparks skittered across the tiles, hot enough that he felt the heat on his shins. His feet skidded. Momentum stole his balance for a second — then he caught himself, twisting hard as he slammed shoulder-first into the next corner and careened down a new hallway. One of the keys flicked out of his grip mid-turn, bounced once, and slid across the linoleum with a traitorous rattle. “Shit—!” He spun out wide, snatched it back up in a near dive, and didn’t pause to check for damage. The seconds were bleeding . He needed to lose him. Somehow. Loop a vault. Take a back route. Anything. But Léry’s didn’t offer clean chase paths. Just rows of crumbling treatment rooms, cluttered therapy spaces, wheelchairs left to
